subject: Culture
title: Green Burials
description: A micro-lesson that makes Green Burials usable.

hook.text: A company in Washington state turns human remains into soil in 30 days. Your body becomes a garden.

buildup.text: Traditional US burials use 4.3 million gallons of embalming fluid and 20 million board feet of hardwood annually.

discovery.text: Green burials skip embalming, use biodegradable shrouds, and let the body decompose naturally into the earth.

twist.text: Jewish and Muslim burials have always been green—plain shroud, no embalming, buried quickly in contact with soil.

climax.text: Human composting is now legal in several US states. The death industry faces its first disruption in a century.

punchline.text: The greenest funeral is also the oldest one.

quiz.question: How long does human composting take?

details.summary: Green burials skip embalming, use biodegradable coffins or shrouds, and let bodies decompose naturally into the earth. This growing movement rejects the chemical-intensive modern funeral industry in favor of returning the body to nature — an ancient practice repackaged for ecological times.
details.whyItMatters: Green burials challenge the $20 billion funeral industry by offering a simpler, cheaper, and environmentally responsible alternative to conventional burial's chemicals and concrete vaults.
takeaways: Green burials use no embalming chemicals and biodegradable containers
Conventional burial uses formaldehyde-based embalming fluid
Human composting is now legal in several US states

faq.question: What makes a burial green?
faq.answer: Green burial means no embalming (which uses formaldehyde and other toxic chemicals), no metal or concrete vault, and a biodegradable container — a simple wood casket, wicker basket, or linen shroud. The body decomposes naturally, enriching the soil.

faq.question: What is human composting?
faq.answer: Human composting (natural organic reduction) accelerates decomposition by placing the body in a vessel with wood chips, alfalfa, and straw. Over 30-60 days, the body becomes nutrient-rich soil. Washington state legalized it first in 2019.
